properties.description: BUILT 2026-07-25 on Anthony's choice of option (a) from dec:nested-graphs. His case: an organisation builds a satellite capability with a space segment, a ground/user segment and a control segment; his team owns the satellite, and specifically inter-satellite laser communications. He needs to understand the system of systems, but day to day he needs his own part's gaps — not the program's. Every detector until now took the whole design as its subject, which is the unbounded-read failure (cap:bounded-reads) one level up: technically complete, practically unusable, and the human response is to stop looking. `detect_gaps` and `detect_defects` now take `scope` (a node id) and `depth`. FOUND WHILE BUILDING, and it cost a failing test worth keeping: A SCOPE IS NOT A BLAST RADIUS. The first implementation reused the propagation radius on the reasoning that claimed_region and propagate_change already agree what a region is; the test that scoped to a Project and expected the whole design failed, because CONTAINS is deliberately excluded from the traceability rules (propagating along it would make the Project a hub short-circuiting every sibling to two hops). That exclusion is right for IMPACT — a change to a segment does not implicate every screw inside it — and wrong for OWNERSHIP, where a segment lead owns what is inside their segment by definition. So a scope is containment closure (unbounded: ownership does not attenuate with distance) then traceability radius (bounded: the thread reaches into other people's work and must stop). A CONSEQUENCE RECORDED RATHER THAN SILENTLY FIXED: claim_region still uses the radius alone, so claiming a segment does not claim the subsystems inside it — possibly a defect in the claims layer, but changing what a claim covers changes what two people believe they hold, so it is Anthony's call. SECOND FINDING, also from a test: the first filter silently dropped gaps that anchor on nothing — the lifecycle-phase gaps, which are statements about the design as a whole. That was the exact silent-drop this feature exists to prevent, so findings now land in exactly one of four buckets that sum to the total: in_scope, out_of_scope, unanchored, and project_level counted within in_scope. A scoped answer can therefore never imply the rest of the program is clean, and filtering never becomes the tool deciding what a team is allowed to worry about — a project-level rollup still reaches a team when it touches their work, carrying its own scope so they can see whose finding it is. NOT DONE: graph_report is a rollup, not a detector, and scoping it means per-subtree delivery denominators and modularity — a different job, deliberately not smuggled in here.
properties.name: A team asks the detectors about its own part, and is told what it did not see
